extracted.intended_audience: seamen, sailors, ropeworkers, and hobbyists who handle ropes, rigging, cordage, and need practical instruction in knots, lashings, splices, and finishes
extracted.subtask_description: A practical manual describing how to make shortenings, grommets, eyes, lashings, seizings, splices, fancy knots, worming/serving, and temporary halters, with usage notes and construction tips. Focused on step-by-step construction and best practices for maritime ropework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheepshank (shortening) — suitability and security
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheepshanks (Dogshanks) are used for shortening rope, especially where both ends are fast; the best and most secure form is shown in Fig. 78. They will not withstand a very great strain but are secure from untying by accident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sheepshanks to take up spare rope or lashings when ends are fixed. Simpler forms (Fig. 79) are less reliable and 'can hardly be depended upon unless the ends are seized' (Fig. 80). Choose the most secure form for higher reliability; seize ends if greater security is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grommet — required length and making technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The grommet is formed of a single strand of rope five times as long as the circumference of the grommet when complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay one end across the other at the loop size required and follow the lay to form a two-strand ring, then continue twisting to form a three-strand ring. Finish and secure ends with overhand knots, pass ends under nearest strands, and trim close. Keep a strong twist on the strand while 'laying up' to produce a firm, smooth, endless ring comparable to the original rope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selvagee (Sevagee) strap — construction and use
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'Sevagee' or 'Selvagee' strap is a kind of ring made by passing a number of strands or yarns around pins or nails set in a board and binding the whole together with a seizing of yarn or marline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These produce strong, durable straps used for blocks aboard ship, handles to boxes and chests, and similar applications. Use proper seizing to bind securely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flemish Eye — construction and finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: A Flemish Eye is made by laying yarns around a spar or wood the size of the intended eye, fastening them, unlaying and opening rope strands, lapping the yarns over the wood and stops, fastening by overhand knots, worming the free ends under and over, then tying and finishing with whipping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whip all around with yarn or marline to finish neatly. Follow the illustrated sequence (Fig. 90 A/B) to ensure a tidy, durable eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial Eye — method and finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Make an artificial eye by unlaying one strand, placing remaining strands alongside the standing part, passing the loose strand around and through the spaces as in making a grommet until it returns down the standing part and lies under the eye with the strands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide and taper the strands, then whip the whole with yarn or marline (Fig. 94). This method can be quicker and sometimes stronger than a spliced eye.

rubrics_metrics.name: Throat seizing and lashed rings — quick ring methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Throat Seizing: open the end slightly and lash it to the standing part. Another ring may be made quickly by lashing the two ends of a short rope to the standing part of another (lashed cut-splice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These methods produce useful rings when a free end is available or when a quick, temporary ring is needed. Use appropriate lashing to ensure the ring holds under expected load.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rose (Wedding) lashing — joining eyes or looped ropes
rubrics_metrics.description: The rose lashing (or wedding knot) is used to join two eyes or ropes finished with loops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when you need a secure connection between looped ends; follow the method illustrated (Fig. 97) for correct wrapping and tensioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadeye lashing — standing rigging adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: The deadeye lashing is frequently used on ships' standing rigging; it consists of a small line reeved back and forth through the holes in the deadeyes and seized to the standing rigging to prevent slipping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lashing allows easy and rapid lengthening or shortening of rigging and is especially useful with wire cable. Ensure ends are properly seized to prevent slippage (Fig. 98).

rubrics_metrics.name: Belaying-pin splice — emergency join
rubrics_metrics.description: Belaying-pin splice is a quick and handy way of fastening two ropes together, valuable when rigging is carried away and quick joining of severed ends is required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass a belaying-pin (or toggle) through an eye in one rope and the loop in the broken end, form a loop in the other broken end, pass the lanyard through and around another toggle, haul taut, and fasten by half-hitches or seizing. It is strong, reliable, can be tightened or instantly thrown off (Fig. 100).

rubrics_metrics.name: Necklace tie and Close band — binding side-by-side objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The necklace tie holds two ropes, hawsers, or timbers side by side by passing the lashing around them; ends are secured by a square knot passed around the band lengthwise. The close band is similar but ends are fastened by drawing through beneath the turns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use necklace tie or close band to lash parallel items; ensure turns are even and ends are secured as specified (Figs. 101–102).

rubrics_metrics.name: End pointing (pointed rope) — attractive, functional finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pointing a rope: first whip the end, unlay the end as for a Flemish eye, take out about two-thirds of the yarns and twist each in two to form 'nettles,' comb out remaining yarns leaving a few to lay back, pass three turns of twine like a timber-hitch around where nettles separate, lay nettles back and forth with each turn, whip and finally 'snake' (take the end under and over the outer turns alternately).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If properly done the pointed rope is handsome and less bulky for passing through blocks or eyes. For small rope, inserting a stick in the upper part or finishing tip with a small eye strengthens the point. Alternative simple ending: seize the end, open out strands, bring strands back alongside the rope and whip the whole (Figs. 103–105).

rubrics_metrics.name: Short splice — method and precautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Short splice: untwist the ends for a few inches and seize with twine to prevent unwinding; seize each strand end and grease/wax strands until smooth. Place ends together and pass each strand alternately through the strands of the other rope; then untwist, taper strands, seize, pass reduced strands under whole strands for two or three lays, draw tight and trim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taper strands gradually for an extra-neat splice so the splice is little larger than the original rope. Avoid allowing two strands to run under the same strand of the opposite rope — remember 'the first strand must be passed over the strand which is first next to it and through under the second and out between the second and third' to keep the pattern correct (Fig. 106).

rubrics_metrics.name: Long splice — construction for blocks and smooth running
rubrics_metrics.description: Long splice: unlay the ends about four times as much as for the short splice (about four to five feet), unlay one strand in each rope for half as much again, place middle strands together, work central strands into grooves, cut out half the yarns in certain strands, make overhand knots and tuck ends under lays, then stretch, pound and roll the splice until smooth and trim off loose ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-made long splice will run through any block or tackle which will admit the rope itself and may be indistinguishable from the rope after a few days' use (Fig. 107). Maintain tight twists while laying and taper the ends carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eye splice — forming a permanent loop
rubrics_metrics.description: Eye splice is made like the short splice but the end is bent around and spliced into its own strands of the standing part to form an eye (Fig. 108).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for permanent loops and convenient attachment points; finish by tucking and smoothing as with short splice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cut splice — forming a loop in the centre
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut splice: made like an eye or short splice but with the ends lapped and each spliced into the standing part of the other, forming a loop or eye in the centre of a rope (Fig. 109).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when a central eye is needed rather than an eye at an end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replacing a single worn/broken strand — invisible repair
rubrics_metrics.description: If one strand is worn, frayed, or broken, unlay and cut off the weak strand and lay a new strand of the same length into the groove left by the old strand as in a long splice; taper and stick the ends under the lay as in a short splice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If well done the repair will never show and will be as strong as the original rope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single Crown — uses and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Single Crown knot: simplest fancy knot; made by unlaying strands and interweaving them in a specific order. It is 'a very poor knot to stand by itself' and is mainly valuable as a basis for other more complicated knots or for ending up rope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To finish a rope with a crown, leave projecting ends long, bring them down and tuck under strands of the standing part, halve and tuck again until neat (Figs. 110–113). Crown endings will not work loose like a seizing and are quicker to form when small stuff is not at hand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wall knot — construction and role
rubrics_metrics.description: Wall knot is practically a crown reversed; make by bringing strands over and through specified bights, then draw snug; ends may be trimmed or tucked and tapered as in the crown (Figs. 114–116).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valuable as an ending and as a basis for ornamental knots; use as starting element for shroud knots and combined wall-and-crown forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shroud knots (common and French) — method and finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Common shroud knot: open strands as for short splice, place two ends together, single 'wall' the strands of one rope around the standing part of another against the lay, taper ends and tuck and serve with yarn. French shroud knot: more complex but 'far neater and better' — involves looping and passing strand ends through bights in a sequence, drawing taut, tapering, tucking and serving (Figs. 117–120).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serve carefully after tucking for a neat, durable finish. Use French shroud knot when appearance and neatness are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double wall, Double crown, and Wall crowned — decorative endings
rubrics_metrics.description: Double wall and double crown are made like the single forms but carried around a second time following the lay; crowning a wall produces a crown above the wall. These produce decorative and robust rope-ends (Figs. 121–125).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ends may be tucked or trimmed; crowning improves effect. Follow the lay closely and work slack appropriately to tuck strands so there is no visible beginning or end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double wall and crown (Manrope knot) — usage and invisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The Double Wall and Crown (Manrope knot) is made by making a single wall and crown, leaving strands slack, passing ends up and through the bights and down through the walling, then tightening. If properly done and ends tapered and tucked there will be no sign of a beginning or ending to this knot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for finishing ends of rope railings, man-ropes, yoke-lines, and to form stoppers or toggles. Produces an elegant, almost seamless finish (Figs. 126–130).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matthew Walker (Stopper knot) — stopper properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Matthew Walker (Stopper knot): formed by passing each strand in turn through bights of others according to a pattern; when hauled taut the knot becomes 'hard, close, and presents an almost flat shoulder on its lower side.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well suited as a stopper on rope ends where they pass through holes (bucket handles, trap-door handles, chest handles). Learn the sequence carefully (Figs. 131–133) to achieve the characteristic compact shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turk's Head — ornamental uses and method
rubrics_metrics.description: Turk's Head is an ornamental knot used to ornament rigging, form shoulders or rings on stays or ropes, ornament yoke-lines, form slip-collars on lanyards, collar stanchions or spars, and as a neckerchief fastener when made of small line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make around a smooth round stick with closely twisted or braided small line, follow the lay and braid two or more lays until complete, then work up slack and draw bights taut. A variation (Turk's cap) can be formed by slipping the knot to the end of the rod and working one side tighter to form a cap (Figs. 135–137).

rubrics_metrics.name: Worming, Parcelling, and Serving — smoothing and protecting ropes
rubrics_metrics.description: Worming: twist a small line into the grooves between the strands to fill grooves. Parcelling: cover the rope already wormed with a strip of canvas wound spirally with overlapping edges. Serving: wrap the rope with spun yarn, marline, or other small stuff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a serving mallet to work tighter and more evenly. Always stretch the rope tightly between two uprights before serving. Parcelling is optional for ordinary purposes but provides extra protection; half-hitch serving is a decorative variation (Fig. 138–140).

rubrics_metrics.name: Half-hitch serving — decorative spiral serving
rubrics_metrics.description: Half-hitch work: take a half-hitch around the rope, then another below it, draw snug, repeat until the object is covered; the series of half-hitches forms a spiral twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very pretty when well done; several lines of half-hitches can be used simultaneously for varied effects (Figs. 139–140).

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-strand braid and Crown-braid — ornamental braiding
rubrics_metrics.description: Four-strand braiding consists in crossing the opposite strands across and past one another. Crown-braid is formed like ordinary crowning and may be done with any number of strands (four or six are common).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces highly ornamental finishes; practice with fewer strands before attempting many (Figs. 141–143).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rope buckles, swivels, slings, and rope belting — applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Rope can be used to form buckles, swivels, and slings; in factories or machine shops rope belting may be preferable to leather and, if well spliced, will run smoothly even on long stretches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate splicing and finishing so belting runs evenly; splices and toggles illustrated (Figs. 144–148, 128–130) show common useful attachments and stoppers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary halter for animals — bowline-based construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporary halter: make by putting the end of a long rope around the animal's neck and tying a common bowline knot; follow with a second loop passed around the animal's head twice and under the first loop, then adjust to pass over forelock and ears to complete the halter (Figs. 149–154).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bowline provides secure loop; ensure second loop is long enough to pass over ears and forelock. Use only as a temporary halter and follow the step sequence to avoid choking or slipping.
